7
Two masses, M and m, are connected by an inextensible string which passes over a frictionless
pulley. Mass M rests on a frictionless slope, as shown.
M
m
frictionless slope
θ
The slope is at an angle θ to the horizontal.
The two masses are initially held stationary and then released. Mass M moves down the slope.
Which expression must be correct?
m
A
sinθ < M
m
B
cosθ < M
m
C
sinθ > M
m
D
cosθ > M

hints: Look at mass $M$ on the angle $\theta$ slope: only the component of its weight parallel to the slope can pull it down the slope.
Use the observed motion: $M$ moves down the slope and $m$ moves up, so the pull down the slope must be larger than the weight hanging vertically.
Write the down-slope pull as $Mg\sin\theta$ and the opposing pull as $mg$, then divide the inequality by $Mg$ to get $\sin\theta$ compared with $m/M$.
walkthrough: Identify the two weights: $Mg$ vertically down for the block on the slope and $mg$ vertically down for the hanging mass.
Resolve the weight of $M$ parallel to the frictionless slope. The component acting down the slope is $Mg\sin\theta$, while $Mg\cos\theta$ acts into the slope.
Apply motion along the string. Because the string is inextensible, both masses have the same speed. Since $M$ moves down the slope after release, the system accelerates in that direction.

For acceleration down the slope, the resultant force must act down the slope, so the down-slope pull must be greater than the tension pull from $m$. At the instant of release this requires $Mg\sin\theta > mg$.
Cancel $g$ and rearrange: divide both sides by $M$ to get $g\sin\theta > (m/M)g$, so $\sin\theta > m/M$. This is option C.

A.explanation: This reverses the inequality. If $\sin\theta$ were less than $m/M$, the hanging weight would win and $M$ would move up the slope.

B.explanation: The down-slope component uses $\sin\theta$, not $\cos\theta$. $Mg\cos\theta$ is the component normal to the slope.

C.explanation: For $M$ to accelerate down the slope, the down-slope component $Mg\sin\theta$ must exceed the hanging weight $mg$, giving $\sin\theta > m/M$.

D.explanation: The normal component $Mg\cos\theta$ does not pull along the slope, so $\cos\theta > m/M$ does not describe the motion along the string.
